title: How an 1876 Massacre of Black Men in South Carolina Turned Racial Terror into Political Power
author: Jacob Ware
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Hamburg_cartoon-680x489.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/06/how-
an-1876-massacre-of-black-men-in-south-carolina-turned-racial-terror-into-
political-power/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Hamburg_cartoon-680x489.jpg)

Cartoon decrying the Hamburg massacre of July 1876

As the [U.S. celebrates its 250th
anniversary](https://theconversation.com/topics/america-250-186108), its
citizens commemorate a democracy more diverse, free and inclusive than it’s
ever been. The path to this milestone was imperfect and paved in [blood and
suffering](https://segregationinamerica.eji.org/report/from-slavery-to-
segregation.html). Still, few of the revelers will likely pay heed to the
anniversary of another historic event: the 150th anniversary of the July 1876
[Hamburg massacre](https://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/neatline/show/after-slavery-
hamburg-massacre).

The massacre, which took place in Hamburg, South Carolina, began as a dispute
between a local Black militia and two white citizens over whether the latter
could cross the group’s centennial Fourth of July parade. The militia leader,
[Doc Adams](https://www.scencyclopedia.org/sce/entries/hamburg-massacre/), was
later [charged with blocking a public
highway](https://www.zinnedproject.org/news/tdih/hamburg-massacre/).

[At his court hearing](https://www.thestate.com/news/politics-
government/article263281683.html), Adams was met with a white militia – part
of the white supremacist [Red Shirts](https://www.charlestonmuseum.org/news-
events/waving-the-bloody-shirt-reconstruction-era-violence-and-political-
identity/) – which then pursued the Black militia on their retreat to their
weapons arsenal. After a firefight, the Red Shirts captured several Black
militiamen, marched them to a nearby site and [executed at least four
people](https://www.scencyclopedia.org/sce/entries/hamburg-massacre/).

South Carolina’s Republican governor, [Union veteran Daniel Henry
Chamberlain](https://ronchernow.com/grant/), described the event as a
“butchery of unoffending and unarmed colored men by a brutal and bloodthirsty
mob of white men.” Yet [no one was
convicted](https://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/neatline/show/after-slavery-hamburg-
massacre) after the attack. In fact, several of the Red Shirts ringleaders
[would instead rise](https://www.charlestonmuseum.org/news-events/waving-the-
bloody-shirt-reconstruction-era-violence-and-political-identity/) to the
highest offices in the state.

Corey Rogers, an organizer of the [150th anniversary Hamburg
commemoration](https://www.wrdw.com/video/2026/06/25/hamburg-massacre-150th-
anniversary/), recently called this massacre “the seminal event that began to
change the trajectory of African Americans.” The [repression and
inequality](https://www.illiberalism.org/illiberalism-a-conceptual-
introduction/) that would define the next 100 years of U.S. history, in other
words, was born at Hamburg.

As [a scholar of domestic
terrorism](https://cjc.georgetown.edu/profiles/jacob-ware/), I study the long
history of white supremacist and far-right violence in the U.S. [My
research](https://www.mccaininstitute.org/about/nsct-
fellows-2026-cohort/jacob-ware/) shows that the Hamburg massacre was not just
characteristic of a broader violent moment, but also that the echoes of such
violence [ring loudly today](https://cup.columbia.edu/book/god-guns-and-
sedition/9780231558808/).

**From Hamburg, across the South**

[According to one estimate](https://eji.org/report/reconstruction-in-
america/documenting-reconstruction-violence/), the 12 years of the
Reconstruction era, during which the Union attempted to construct a racially
diverse democracy in the wake of the Civil War, saw over 2,000 Black citizens
murdered in “racial terror lynchings.” [Another estimate, from
1895](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/feb/22/us-white-supremacy-
democracy-capitol-attack), more starkly claimed that as many as 53,000 Black
Americans had been murdered in the 30 years following the Civil War.

By intimidating Black voters and galvanizing white Democrats who sought to
undo the results of the Civil War, this violence [served to effectively kill
Reconstruction](https://www.thestate.com/news/politics-
government/article263281683.html) and the tangible promises of Black
emancipation.

What happened in Hamburg provides a particularly egregious example of such
racial terrorism catapulting political triumph. After that tragedy, several of
the Red Shirts ringleaders went on to successful political careers, with [two
of them becoming U.S. senators](https://www.charlestonmuseum.org/news-
events/waving-the-bloody-shirt-reconstruction-era-violence-and-political-
identity/) – one of whom, Benjamin Tillman, also served as South Carolina
governor.

As Jenny Heckel, then a Clemson University graduate student, [noted in her
2016 master’s thesis](https://open.clemson.edu/all_theses/2558/), it was “not
in spite of the white Carolinians’ participation in the murder of six black
men, but because of it, they won election to political offices.”

In South Carolina’s 1876 gubernatorial race, the Democratic candidate,
Confederate veteran Wade Hampton III, emerged triumphant and reinstated white
supremacy as the [fulcrum of state
governance](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3070159). His name [had been put
forward](https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1876/08/13/81696647.html?pageNumber=2)
by former Confederate major general Matthew Butler, who had [represented the
two white farmers](https://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/neatline/show/after-slavery-
hamburg-massacre) before the Hamburg attack and who himself went on to serve
in the U.S. Senate.

In 1895, South Carolina held a [constitutional
convention](https://calendar.eji.org/racial-injustice/sep/11), spearheaded by
the aforementioned Hamburg massacre ringleader Tillman, and adopted a new
constitution that effectively ended the Black vote in the state.

**An enduring threat**

In the 1890s, renowned abolitionist and orator [Frederick
Douglass](https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/frederick-douglass) said white
vigilantes offered [three justifications](https://time.com/6977494/far-right-
terrorism-reconstruction-era-essay/) for the lynchings of Black Americans:
stamping out alleged race riots, protecting the white vote share and
protecting white women from alleged sexual crimes by Black men.

The first two were front and center in the Hamburg massacre. [In fact, as
Heckel reflected](https://open.clemson.edu/all_theses/2558/) a decade ago,
“white Carolinians blamed the black militia for starting the riot, and
Southern white newspapers created images of riotous blacks to contest black
descriptions.”

![A black-and-white image of a man in a suit and bow
tie](https://images.theconversation.com/files/751219/original/file-20260730-50-shf53y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)Abolitionist
and orator Frederick Douglass said white mobs often justified lynchings as a
response to riots, to Black voting and to alleged crimes against white women.  
[Library of Congress/Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-
photo/american-journalist-author-former-slave-and-abolitionist-news-
photo/3324112?slot=2&adppopup=true)

Since the massacre, racial violence has had a long echo in the United States.
And in many cases, the same justifications elucidated by Douglass remain.

Both the Tulsa race massacre and the 1955 murder of Emmett Till, for instance,
were [sparked by false accusations](https://slate.com/news-and-
politics/2015/06/the-deadly-history-of-theyre-raping-our-women-racists-have-
long-defended-their-worst-crimes-in-the-name-of-defending-white-womens-
honor.html) of sexual harassment or assault made against young Black men.

The violence persists today. In June 2015, just 150 miles (241 kilometers)
from Hamburg, a white supremacist gunman entered the historically Black
[Mother Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal
Church](https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2016/06/08/481149042/how-a-
shooting-changed-charlestons-oldest-black-church) in Charleston, South
Carolina, and opened fire, [killing nine
churchgoers](https://www.scetv.org/emanuelnine#/rounds/1/gallery).

In May 2022, a white supremacist [killed 10 Black
Americans](https://theconversation.com/replacement-theory-isnt-new-3-things-
to-know-about-how-this-once-fringe-conspiracy-has-become-more-
mainstream-183492) at the Tops Friendly Market in Buffalo, New York.

Both gunmen made multiple references to the same conspiracy theories Douglass
identified, with the Charleston [domestic
terrorist](https://journals.law.harvard.edu/jol/wp-
content/uploads/sites/86/2017/03/54.1-HLL105.pdf) going as far as to [praise
segregation](https://time.com/6977494/far-right-terrorism-reconstruction-era-
essay/) as “a defensive measure” [while
criticizing](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2015/jun/20/dylann-roof-fbi-
website-manifesto-charleston-shooting) the “historical lies, exaggerations and
myths” of the historical record of slavery and its aftermath.

Still, there are key differences between the attacks at Charleston and Buffalo
and their Reconstruction predecessors. The [political
violence](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/reconstruction-
southern-violence-during-reconstruction/) that tainted the Reconstruction and
post-Reconstruction era clashes with traditional definitions of terrorism,
which typically targets a power structure that such violence seeks to upend.

Instead, attacks like the one in Hamburg, which sought to proactively protect
the rights and power of white Americans – and which were often endorsed by
state and local governments – have more in common with genocide and ethnic
cleansing. Not only did the scale of the [broader violence across the
South](https://doi.org/10.1162/isec_a_00410) indicate a campaign to mass-
murder an ethnic subgroup for political purposes, but Tillman, perhaps the
most infamous of the Hamburg murderers, [never
denied](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/feb/22/us-white-supremacy-
democracy-capitol-attack) the attack’s goals.

“We are not sorry for it,” he would proudly recall before the U.S. Senate in
1900. “We of the south have never recognized the right of the negro to govern
white men.”

**‘A painful duty’**

Attempting to commemorate all such anniversaries is an impossible task, simply
because of the sheer volume. For example, September marks the 150th
anniversary of the [Ellenton
Riot](https://www.scencyclopedia.org/sce/entries/ellenton-riot/). In that
massacre, Black South Carolinians were systematically hunted throughout their
community over an alleged attack on a white elderly woman, which was later
proved false. The death toll may have eclipsed 100.

[Countless similar incidents](https://www.britannica.com/topic/list-of-race-
riots-and-massacres-in-the-United-States) have plagued U.S. history.

In my view, to tell the story of America’s founding without referencing these
profound scars is akin to deceit, if not complicity. [Civil rights leader and
journalist Ida B.
Wells](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/14977/14977-h/14977-h.htm) put it this
way in 1895: “It becomes a painful duty … to reproduce a record which shows
that a large portion of the American people avow anarchy, condone murder and
defy the contempt of civilization.”

Or, as a [local retired
pastor](https://www.postandcourier.com/northaugusta/community/hamburg-
massacre-north-augusta-commemoration-events-
clyburn/article_39b6fd4b-616a-4a79-ac4e-43c8a3351d38.html) said of Hamburg
commemorations, “We want to keep it burning so people won’t forget what
transpired.”![The
Conversation](https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287285/count.gif?distributor=republish-
lightbox-basic)
